title: 7 Boring Habits That Will Take You From Good to Great
author: Jain, Gaurav
summary: Gaurav Jain argues that effective leadership is produced not by dramatic insight but by seven unglamorous, easily-skipped daily and weekly routines practiced consistently over time. He works through each habit in turn — writing down three daily priorities before opening email or Slack, blocking dedicated weekly thinking time, asking the same three questions in every one-on-one, closing every meeting with a named owner and deadline, sending one genuine weekly thank-you, auditing the past week's calendar against the Eisenhower Matrix, and reading one leadership idea per week — explaining for each why the routine matters and what breaks down without it. His recurring argument is that a leader's actual priorities are revealed by their calendar rather than their stated intentions, which is why several of the habits (the daily top-three, the weekly audit) are explicitly calendar-based interventions. The piece closes by naming its own thesis directly: leadership is repetitive rather than glamorous, and its compounding power comes from consistency rather than any single high-impact decision.
points: Writing down three daily priorities before checking Slack, email, or meetings is framed as a way to stop the calendar from leading the person rather than the reverse.

Asking the same three fixed questions ('What's working? What's frustrating? What do you need from me?') in every one-on-one is argued to surface small issues before they escalate, rather than requiring a fresh agenda each time.
Ending every meeting by naming who is doing what by when is presented as a two-minute investment that prevents hours of downstream confusion and passive-aggressive follow-up.
The weekly calendar audit explicitly runs the past week's activities through the Eisenhower Matrix (urgent/important quadrants) to decide what to do, schedule, delegate, or delete going forward.
The essay's overall thesis is stated directly: leadership is not built in moments of brilliance but in the repetition of boringly simple habits that compound over time.
quotes: As leaders, we chase shiny. We chase fast. And, we chase what's new. But the secret to great leadership is not the shiny ideas. It's the boring stuff.
Most leaders I talk to wake up and dive into Slack, email, or meetings. That's not you leading. That's your calendar leading you.
Try these three questions every single time: What's working? What's frustrating? What do you need from me?
I've been to countless meetings that were a complete waste of everyone's time because they failed to ask a simple question at the end: "Who's doing what, by when?
no matter what you say, your calendar represents your real priorities and what you care about. Don't just fill it, fix it.
Leadership is not built in moments of brilliance. It's built in repetition, day in and day out, of boringly simple habits.
